title: What level, reputation and governance model makes progression meaningful without becoming school?
summary: Prior art: Stack Overflow privileges, Reddit karma and mod tooling, Wikipedia governance, Discord roles, Duolingo and Khan progression, university numbering. Levels as progression not uniformity; automatic tracking; badges; user-created subtopics with reputation gates; appeals; AI-assisted moderation; owner keeps final authority.

title: Stack Overflow ties privileges to reputation thresholds, published on /help/privileges
summary: Reputation gates actions: vote up at 15, comment/flag at 50, vote down at 125, edit others posts and review queues around 2000, create tags near 3000, moderator tools and analytics at 10000, protect questions at 15000, trusted-user delete/undelete at 20000. The official blog names 500/1k/2k/3k/10k as the meaningful jumps; the canonical /help/privileges page could not be fetched by this tool (blocked domain), so mid-range figures rest on third-party mirrors, not the primary page directly.

title: Stack Overflow traffic and new questions collapsed after ChatGPT, roughly halving 2022 to 2025
summary: Monthly visits fell from about 110M in 2022 to about 55M by 2024 (~50 percent). New questions fell from 87000/month in March 2023 to 58800 in March 2024 (-32.5 percent); Wikipedia cites a further 78 percent fall Dec 2024 to Dec 2025, down from a 2014 peak near 200000/month. The company cut 38 percent of staff across two 2023 rounds, then licensed its content to OpenAI in May 2024 -- the same tool credited with the traffic loss.

title: Stack Overflow decline reads as a moderation-culture failure a reputation formula enabled, not just AI substitution
summary: AI substitution (faster, more polite) is well evidenced but incomplete: closed-as-duplicate gatekeeping was a top community complaint for a decade before ChatGPT existed. Reputation rewarded fast terse answers and closing/downvoting over patient teaching, selecting for the exact tone a friendlier alternative could beat instantly. Lesson: a reputation formula is a selection pressure on TONE, not just a leaderboard -- reward welcoming, teaching-shaped contributions explicitly or tone drifts toward whatever the formula actually pays for.

title: Reddit karma is an opaque, sitewide, non-1:1 function of votes, undocumented by design
summary: Reddit Help confirms karma reflects upvotes/downvotes but explicitly withholds the exact formula; updates are deliberately delayed and randomized to resist manipulation. Karma is sitewide, not topic-scoped, split into post and comment karma, and self-votes are blocked by the UI though the formula itself is unaudited. The real anti-spam gate is layered locally: many subreddits require a minimum account age and karma total, set per-subreddit by mods, before allowing a post or comment.

title: The 2023 Reddit API-pricing revolt saw over 7800 subreddits go dark
summary: Reddit announced paid API pricing that would kill third-party apps (Apollo, RIF); moderators of 7000-plus subreddits (one count: 7808 planned, run by 28000-plus volunteers) set communities private starting June 12 2023. It is the clearest large-scale proof volunteer moderators can coordinate to disrupt a platform materially -- and that the platform can override them: Reddit adjusted mod-removal tooling and threatened to replace holdout moderators, which several subreddits read as proof community governance is subordinate whenever it truly conflicts with revenue.

title: Wikipedia governance runs on RfA (adminship by consensus vote), ArbCom (final dispute court), and written policy, not reputation points
summary: Admin rights come only through Requests for Adminship, a public consensus discussion (or, since 2024, periodic administrator elections) run by the community; only bureaucrats can flip the bit after consensus. The Arbitration Committee is the final binding step for conduct disputes policy cannot resolve. There is no numeric reputation score anywhere in this stack -- authority is earned through a public track record editors vote on directly, which is higher-friction than a threshold but harder to game with volume alone.

title: Wikipedia active-editor decline: peak near 90000 in early 2007, roughly 37000 in the most recent month checked
summary: Wikipedia:Statistics states users with 5-plus edits number 3.7 million total, 37167 in the last month (page checked 2026-09-04, exact snapshot date on-page unclear). Multiple secondary sources (MIT Technology Review; the deletionism article) put the active-editor peak between about 51000 and 90000+ around 2007, before a sustained decline attributed partly to deletion-discussion hostility toward new contributors ("newbie biting"). The two peak figures disagree by nearly 2x depending on source methodology -- flagged, not resolved, here.

title: Wikipedia deletionist-inclusionist wars: notability rules alienated novice contributors and are linked to the editor decline
summary: Deletionists favor strict notability/sourcing gates; inclusionists favor broad retention for future improvement. Secondary sources tie aggressive deletion-discussion culture in the mid-to-late 2000s to a demotivating effect on new editors, contributing to the active-editor decline from its 2007 peak -- described as a self-reinforcing downward spiral where preemptive deletion discouraged the very participation the encyclopedia needed to keep growing.

title: Discord permissions are role-based and positional: a role only ever governs roles below it in one ordered list
summary: Discord roles carry a position value; the highest role a member holds sets their effective rank, and a role (or bot) can only grant, edit, or moderate roles positioned below its own highest role -- never lateral or upward. Permissions resolve in a fixed order: base @everyone at guild level, then role grants at guild level, then channel-level overwrites (deny before allow). No reputation or activity signal is involved; all authority is manually assigned by someone already above you in the hierarchy.

title: Duolingo progression stacks streaks, XP/leagues and skill mastery, and streaks now show strong retention numbers
summary: Per Duolingo shareholder letters and engineering data: over 10 million users held 365-day-plus streaks by end of 2024/early 2026, and daily learners holding 7-plus-day streaks doubled year over year to over half of DAUs. Western-market churn fell from 47 percent (2020) to 28 percent (2024), attributed partly to streak/gamification mechanics. Streak freezes are sold as monetized loss-aversion insurance; the mechanic is criticized as a dark pattern that optimizes for daily app-opens (a vanity/gamed signal), not for language mastery, and can be maintained via trivial one-exercise sessions.

title: Khan Academy separates Mastery (what you know) from Energy Points (effort/engagement) explicitly
summary: Khan Academys own help center distinguishes Mastery levels (Attempted, Familiar, Proficient, Mastered per skill, rolling up to course/unit mastery percentage) from Energy Points, which reward effort -- answering correctly earns 50 points in a mastery challenge, 5 for a previously-mastered skill -- and are explicitly stated to NOT measure mastery or ability. Badges layer on top for community/behavior goals (e.g., building community, learning computer science), separate from both. This three-signal split (know / effort / behavior) is the cleanest prior-art precedent for keeping a knowledge level honest against gaming by volume.

title: University course numbering (100/200/300/400) signals prerequisite depth, not a portable competency rubric
summary: 100-level courses are introductory, open to first-years, and carry no prerequisites; 200-level typically requires a 100-level prerequisite; 300-level is advanced-intermediate, usually gated to sophomores+; 400-level is capstone/seminar-style with heavy student ownership. The numbers are locally set per department/institution with no cross-institution standard -- a 300-level course at one school can be easier than a 200-level at another. It signals sequencing WITHIN a curriculum, not an externally comparable skill level, which is the key caution for any platform borrowing the 100/200/300 label.

title: freeCodeCamp/Codecademy certificates function as a signal of self-motivation, not a hiring credential
summary: Consensus across multiple hiring-focused writeups: employers do not treat freeCodeCamp or Codecademy certificates as bootcamp-equivalent or degree-equivalent credentials. What gets candidates hired is the GITHUB-visible project work and commit history produced while earning the certificate, not the certificate PDF itself. The certificate is read as evidence of follow-through and self-teaching capacity -- a weak but nonzero signal -- never as a skills verification employers rely on directly.

title: Scouting BSA rank ladder (7 ranks to Eagle) ties advancement to demonstrated skill plus service plus time-in-role, not points
summary: Ranks run Scout, Tenderfoot, Second Class, First Class, Star, Life, Eagle. Star/Life/Eagle require a minimum merit-badge count (21 for Eagle, 13 specified), minimum TIME in a leadership position, community-service hours, and for Eagle a self-led service project reviewed by a board -- multiple gates, not a single accruing number. Only about 4 percent of Scouts ever reach Eagle. This is the clearest non-school ladder in the prior art: advancement is multi-dimensional (skill + leadership + service + time) and scarce enough at the top to keep meaning intact.

title: Martial-arts belt systems show what a gamed ladder looks like: the McDojo, belts sold on attendance/payment not skill
summary: A McDojo is the industry-recognized pejorative for a school that promotes on a fixed schedule or ability to pay rather than demonstrated skill, turning belts into a retention/monetization mechanic (frequent grading fees) rather than a competency signal. The criticism is structurally identical to the risk in a platform reputation/level system: any authority that both AWARDS the credential and PROFITS from awarding it faster has a built-in incentive to inflate it, and the term exists specifically because enough schools did.

title: Gamification effect sizes in the literature are inflated by short-study bias and should be read as an upper bound, not an MVP guarantee
summary: The same evidence base shows brief interventions producing effect sizes 5x larger than multi-week ones (1.57 vs 0.30) -- exactly the novelty-driven pattern skeptics warn about, and it means most published gamification studies (run over days to weeks) cannot speak to whether badges/levels sustain engagement over the months this platform needs. The large pooled effect sizes (g near 0.8) are real but are dominated by short, high-novelty studies; treat any single number here as evidence gamification CAN work short-term, not evidence it will sustain a community over a year.

title: Two recent peer-reviewed meta-analyses find large positive effects of gamification on learning outcomes (Hedges g near 0.8)
summary: A 2023-2024 wave of meta-analyses (per Wikipedia Gamification of learning, summarizing peer-reviewed sources): one across 41 studies/5071 participants found g=0.822; another across 22 experimental studies found g=0.782 -- both large effects by Cohen convention. An earlier 2021 PMC meta-analysis (behavioral change specifically) found a smaller, still-significant d=0.48, 95% CI [0.33, 0.62]. Effect size varied strongly by context: brief interventions (days, ES=1.57) beat long ones (up to 20 weeks, ES=0.30); adult/higher-ed (ES=0.95) beat K-12 (ES=0.92).

title: A level should be a rubric of what you can DO, and 1-5 is the right scale for a topic-agnostic ladder
summary: 1-3 is too coarse to feel like progress; 1-10 or academic hundreds invite false cross-topic equivalence (a 300-level course and a hobby-topic Level 3 read as comparable when the university-numbering entry shows they are not, even within one institution). 1-5 leaves room for a real rubric per rung -- e.g. L1 completed intro, L2 first accepted contribution, L3 helped another user get unstuck, L4 created accepted subtopic content, L5 recognized topic leader -- without pretending dozens of intermediate states exist. The scale is cheap to change later; the RUBRIC per rung is the expensive part, since content and badges get built against it.

title: Automatic level tracking must reward outcome signals, not time-on-task or volume -- Khan Academy already proves the split works
summary: Honest signals: completed intro (binary, gameable only by clicking through, low stakes), an accepted contribution (someone else validated it), an answer marked helpful by its asker, a subtopic that survived moderation. Dishonest signals: time-on-task (afk tabs, video autoplay), raw post/comment volume (Stack Overflow selected for exactly this), page views. Khan Academys own split of Mastery (skill) from Energy Points (effort, explicitly NOT mastery) is the cleanest existing proof this separation is buildable and legible to users.

title: Level 1 should require a real action past the 10-minute intro, or the intro should stay explicitly unleveled
summary: The brief already states this (S15: the intro does not necessarily award Level 1). Duolingo and Khan Academy both give immediate, generous feedback for showing up (streak day 1, first energy points) precisely because the FIRST session must feel rewarding -- but neither calls that a level or mastery rank. The honest pattern: reward the intro with something ungated and low-stakes (a completion mark, not a level), and reserve Level 1 for one small demonstrated action after it -- e.g. one accepted edit, one question answered, one project posted. That keeps entry easy while keeping Level 1 meaning something.

title: Levels should be invisible during ordinary browsing and surface only on profiles, contribution UI, and moderation gates
summary: Showing a level badge on every comment (Reddit flair, forum rank badges) visibly stratifies a conversation and biases how replies get read regardless of content quality -- the exact effect Stack Overflow reputation has on answer voting (higher-rep answers get upvoted faster independent of correctness, a documented anchoring effect in reputation-system literature). Recommended surfaces: the users own profile, a create/moderate action explicitly gated by level (so it explains itself only when it matters), and voluntary opt-in display like the Anonymous - Level 5 JavaScript pattern the brief names -- never a persistent badge stamped on every post in a normal thread.

title: Stack Exchange voting shows a documented reputation Matthew effect: high-rep users answers get voted up faster independent of quality
summary: PLOS One (Anderson-Cornwell / Movshovitz-Attias et al framing) The myopia of crowds: Cognitive load and collective evaluation of answers on Stack Exchange documents that answer position, early votes, and answerer reputation bias subsequent voting -- a Matthew effect where early reputation compounds via upvotes largely independent of answer correctness, and accepted-answer status pulls votes toward it even against a rival answer with an equal or higher pre-acceptance score. This is the primary source for the anchoring claim used elsewhere in this log; cited here directly rather than left as an unsourced aside.

title: Reputation must be topic-scoped, derived from an append-only log, never a stored column
summary: public/notes/auth/readme.md S5 argues points-are-derived for likes and generalizes directly: a stored reputation column is a cache with no invalidation story (delete an action, revoke a self-award, fix a scoring bug -- every one needs a compensating write nobody remembers to make). Reputation = SUM(weight) over actions in a log, scoped by topic id, computed on read or materialized as a rebuildable cache only once a measurement demands it. This also makes topic-scoping free: the same log filtered by topic_id IS the topic reputation, with no separate table per topic.

title: Reputation should pay for validated contribution, never popularity or volume alone
summary: Earn: an edit/answer accepted by someone else, a subtopic that survives moderation, a report a moderator upholds, tips received. Must NOT earn: raw post count, unfloored upvotes (a popularity contest), views, time-on-site. The auth readme S5 one-like-per-user-per-page constraint (enforced by a DB primary key, not app code) is the template: reputation-earning actions need the same enforced constraint -- one vote per user per item, and no reputation from actions on your own content, which needs an authorship mapping the auth readme flags as not yet built.

title: Should reputation decay -- nobody in the prior art actually does it, and the case is unevidenced either way
summary: None of the platforms researched (Stack Overflow, Reddit karma, Wikipedia -- which has no numeric reputation at all) decay reputation over time. The argument FOR decay (stale experts squatting on old-topic authority) is plausible but unevidenced; the argument against (it punishes the long-term contributors a topic most needs to retain, and adds a background job that must run correctly forever) is simpler to defend. Recommendation: skip decay for the MVP and revisit only if squatting is observed.

title: Anonymous - Level 5 JavaScript risks laundering sockpuppet reputation, not just deanonymization
summary: The users topic covers deanonymization risk; the community-side risk is different: if anonymous identity persists across a session/device rather than being genuinely single-use, it becomes a second account a banned or downvoted user can walk away from and restart clean -- defeating whatever the reputation gate on subtopic/mod creation was meant to prevent. Reddits account-age-plus-karma subreddit gates suggest anonymous reputation should never itself unlock CREATION privileges (subtopics, moderation) -- only signed-in, harder-to-launder reputation should gate those; anonymous levels stay display-only.

title: The owner-as-constitution rule: the platform can always override, but every override should be visible in the same audit log a mod action is
summary: The Reddit mod-revolt entry shows what happens when platform authority acts invisibly against community expectation (perceived betrayal, mass blackout). The sentence a user would accept: The owner can reverse any moderation decision, and every reversal is logged the same way a mod action is -- nothing disappears silently. Wikipedias ArbCom is the inverse extreme (community-run court with no single owner override) and works only at Wikipedias unique scale and nonprofit structure; a single-owner MVP platform cannot and should not copy it, but SHOULD copy its transparency: every governance action, including owner overrides, in one visible audit trail.

title: Topic ownership should start founder-based (first mover) with reputation-gated moderator ADDITION, never founder-only forever
summary: Elected ownership (Wikipedia RfA-style) needs a large enough active community to hold a real election, which no single new topic will have on day one. Founder-only-forever risks the McDojo failure mode: one persons incentives (or absence) determine the topics fate indefinitely with no correction mechanism. MVP-honest middle: the founding creator is topic owner by default; once a topic has enough distinct high-reputation contributors (a number to set empirically, not guess), the OWNER can promote co-moderators, and only the platform owner can remove a topic owner for cause -- no community vote required or possible yet.

title: Reputation-gated moderation privileges should unlock in stages, mirroring Stack Overflows threshold ladder, not a single mod/not-mod bit
summary: Stack Overflows staged model (flag at 50, edit others posts near 2000, moderator tools at 10000) is the strongest prior-art evidence that graduated privilege works better than a binary admin flag: each threshold is a small trust increment the community can observe being earned. Recommended staged privileges for a topic: report/flag content (low threshold), suggest edits (mid), approve suggested edits and remove spam (higher), full moderation including user bans (topic-owner-granted only, reputation is necessary but not sufficient).

title: AI-assisted triage belongs BEFORE human moderation, as a pre-filter and suggestion, never as the final removal decision in the MVP
summary: The brief places AI moderation cost analysis in the ai research topic; here it is a flow placement question. Recommended flow: report submitted -> AI classifies severity/category and suggests an action -> queued for the lowest-reputation-appropriate human moderator with the AI suggestion visible -> human decides -> action logged with both the AI suggestion and human decision, so drift between the two is auditable and downgradeable to fully-manual if the AI proves unreliable. Never let AI auto-remove content in the MVP; auto-flag-for-review only.

title: Removal needs a visible appeal step or moderation reads as authoritarian -- Wikipedias deletion-review process is the template, simplified
summary: The deletionist-wars entry shows what happens without one: perceived-arbitrary removal drove away exactly the contributors a young community needs most. Minimum honest appeal flow for an MVP: removal always states a reason (even one line), the author can request review, and ANY appeal goes to a person other than the original remover (even if that person is the single MVP moderator days later, having the log entry to reconsider matters more than a different reviewer). No promise of permanence -- content removed for legal/safety reasons stays removed regardless of appeal outcome, and this exception must be stated up front, not discovered.

title: Topic creation MVP: suggest-then-owner-approves, not community voting -- the owner is the only moderator, so voting has nobody to count it
summary: The brief S6 lists community voting for topic creation as one option and the challenge section asks to attack it directly: with exactly one moderator (the owner) in the MVP, a vote has no quorum concept and is theater -- either the owner approves regardless of vote count, or the vote IS the decision and one bad-faith brigade decides a topic. Recommended MVP: any signed-in user can SUGGEST a topic (title + one-line description, stored as a suggestion, not a live page); the owner approves/rejects/merges; approval publishes the page. No voting, no reputation gate on suggesting -- the gate is entirely on publish.

title: Duplicate and typo topics need a redirect-and-merge primitive from day one, or the directory rots within months
summary: Wikipedias notability/deletion machinery exists partly because unmanaged duplicate/near-duplicate articles compound quickly at any real scale. Cheapest honest MVP mechanic: when the owner approves a suggested topic that closely matches an existing slug (string similarity, not AI, for the MVP), offer merge-into-existing as the default action, with redirect the existing page to survive being renamed later, not a new page. Skipping this is fine for the first dozen topics and actively wrong once suggestion volume exceeds one owner reviewing by eye.

title: Top-level topic creation should stay owner-only in the MVP; only subtopic creation should ever be reputation-gated for users
summary: A top-level topic is a first-class site section (per the brief S3, each top-level path is a page/topic) -- getting this wrong is expensive to undo (renaming a live top-level path breaks external links and, per the auth readme, orphans anything keyed on url). Subtopic creation is lower-stakes (nested under an existing owned/moderated topic) and is where reputation-gating and user-driven growth (brief S19) should actually happen. Conflating the two -- letting reputation gate BOTH -- risks a wave of top-level topic spam the moment the gate is met by volume-farming.

title: Badges should be slots, not achievements-for-everything -- specify what earns one and where it shows, leave the art to the owner
summary: Duolingos badge inflation (dozens of achievements for trivial actions) is the childish end the brief explicitly wants to avoid; Khan Academys five-tier badge system tied to real behaviors (mastery, community-building, CS learning) is closer to the target. Recommended MVP slots (3-5 total, not dozens): topic-level rank badge (derived from level, not separately awarded), one contribution badge (first accepted edit/answer), one community badge (helped N people, N small), and a founder/moderator badge (role, not achievement). Every slot ties to a specific, auditable action -- no attendance badges, no daily-login badges (that is the Duolingo streak mechanic, not a badge).

title: The smallest honest progression MVP tracks three things, shows one, and gates one
summary: Track: an append-only action log per user per topic (what happened, when -- the auth readme pattern). Show: a derived level (1-5) and reputation number on the profile and next to create/moderate actions only, never on every post. Gate: exactly one privilege on reputation -- subtopic suggestion -- because it is the one creation action the brief (S19) explicitly wants reputation-gated and it is reversible if wrong (unpublish a bad subtopic; cannot un-ring a moderation-privilege mistake as easily). Everything else (badges, decay, AI triage, elected ownership) waits for the next slice.

title: Challenge: academic 100/200/300/400 numbering as the platforms level scale
summary: Attacking this directly: the university-numbering entry shows the numbers are LOCALLY set per institution with no cross-school standard -- borrowing them imports false authority (a Level 300 topic reads as harder than Level 200 with the same lack of cross-topic comparability the brief already worries about for 1-10, just dressed in academic clothing that implies rigor the platform has not earned). It also signals school exactly when the brief wants the opposite (S35: educational without feeling like school). Verdict: reject academic numbering; see the 1-5 rubric opinion entry for the alternative.

title: Challenge: levels on every topic, including topics that should not have them
summary: Not every topic is progression-shaped (brief S14 already concedes this). A topic that is pure reference material (a single wiki-style article) or pure discussion (a news/current-events space) has no honest content ladder to climb -- forcing a Level system onto it produces exactly the hollow Level 1 for clicking through problem the brief wants to avoid for the intro experience, but for the WHOLE topic. Verdict: levels should be an opt-in topic capability (brief S30: features become plugins/flags), decided by the topic owner at creation, not a default every topic gets.

title: Challenge: reputation as one universal number instead of topic-scoped
summary: A single sitewide number (Reddit karma) is easy to game by volume in whatever topic is cheapest to farm and then spend the resulting authority somewhere unrelated -- exactly the risk brief S29 names (avoid rewarding popularity alone, volume). It also cannot answer the brief S28 question directly: topic-specific reputation may be more meaningful than one universal score is stated as the brief's own working hypothesis. Verdict: agree with the brief -- topic-scoped reputation wins; a single sitewide number should exist ONLY as a lightweight derived sum for profile display, never as anything that gates a privilege.

title: Challenge: community voting for anything in the MVP
summary: Every voting mechanism in the prior art needs either scale (Wikipedia RfA works because thousands of editors can form real consensus) or a clear quorum rule (Reddit subreddit rules, set by mods not by vote-of-the-moment) to avoid being gamed by whoever shows up. An MVP topic will often have single-digit active contributors -- a vote among five people is not community governance, it is whichever five people showed up that day. Verdict: no voting anywhere in the MVP (topic creation, moderation decisions, content curation); owner/moderator decision with a visible appeal path instead, revisit voting once a topic has enough sustained participants that quorum means something.

title: Does gamification help learning, or help engagement metrics that get mistaken for learning -- the evidence genuinely splits here
summary: For: two 2023-2024 meta-analyses show large effect sizes (g=0.78-0.82) on learning OUTCOMES specifically, not just engagement (see the gamification-effect-size finding). Against: those same studies show effect size collapsing by 5x for interventions longer than a few weeks (1.57 to 0.30), and critics (Ian Bogost, cited via Wikipedia) argue point/badge systems measure engagement with the game layer, not the underlying skill, and can crowd out intrinsic motivation over time. Nobody has a long-horizon (6-month-plus) randomized study of a real community platform, as opposed to a classroom intervention -- that gap is the honest answer.

title: Neither imagine/game nor imagine/team sketches an actual level/reputation system -- both are progression-flavored, not progression-mechanic
summary: imagine/game is a Zork-style text adventure using page-tree navigation as the game loop (rooms are pages, exits are links) with no points, levels or reputation at all -- state is inventory/flags in a store. imagine/team is a Kanban board with drag-and-drop task assignment and a load-in-points metric per person, but load is workload capacity, not skill/reputation progression. Neither is prior art for THIS brief; the community topic starts from nothing built, only the auth readmes derived-points principle (S5) to build on.

title: The S33 decision here is the reputation FORMULA, not the level scale -- the scale is relabeling, the formula rewrites history
summary: Changing a level scale from 1-5 to 1-10 later is a pure UI remap (recompute display bands from the same underlying reputation number; nobody's history changes). Changing the REPUTATION FORMULA (what actions earn how much) after users have accumulated reputation under the old formula means either grandfathering two formulas forever (drift, confusion) or recomputing every users historical reputation retroactively (contributions now worth different amounts than when they were made, reading as the platform rewriting the past). The formula is the S33-worthy decision; verdict.md records it.

title: Skeptic pass: the game/team no-prior-art finding has no url by design -- is that acceptable
summary: One established entry (imagine/game and imagine/team have no progression mechanic) carries no url because it is a first-hand code observation, not a claim checkable against an external source -- the writer flags this as advisory. Accepted as-is: the only check available is reading the two page.js files directly, which this researcher did in full before writing the entry; a url would point at the repo itself, which is circular. Downgrading to contested would understate confidence in a direct code read. Left established, flagged here explicitly rather than silently.

title: Skeptic pass: what would falsify the reputation-formula-is-the-hard-to-reverse-choice claim
summary: This entry (S33 subject) would be wrong if a level scale change ALSO forced a retroactive rewrite -- true only if levels were stored as an achieved fact per user rather than derived live from current reputation. The whole point of deriving levels from reputation on read (per the auth-readme-derived-points opinion) is exactly what keeps a scale change cheap; if a future implementation stores level as a fact instead of deriving it, this claim inverts and level-scale becomes the hard-to-reverse one. Recorded so a later implementer who stores levels can see why that choice quietly changes which decision was expensive.

title: Skeptic pass: the Wikipedia active-editor peak figure disagrees by nearly 2x across sources -- left unresolved, not smoothed over
summary: Sources cited elsewhere in this log range from about 51000 to over 90000 for the 2007 peak, depending on whether the source counts 5-plus-edits/month, 100-plus-edits/month, or a different window. This log did not resolve which definition is authoritative -- Wikipedia:Statistics itself uses 5-plus edits for its own current 37167 figure, so the low end of the peak range is the more consistent comparison, but this was not independently re-derived from Wikimedia's raw dataset (stats.wikimedia.org is a JS dashboard this tool cannot fetch). Treat the peak number as directionally right (Wikipedia lost most of its active-editor base since 2007) and not precise to the first significant figure.
